title: Modals, verb patterns and the passive

cards.title: Ability
cards.body: **can / can't** for present ability, **could / couldn't** for general past ability, **be able to** for other tenses and for one specific achievement in the past.
examples: I can speak three languages.
When I was five, I could swim.
I will be able to drive next year.
Despite the traffic, we were able to arrive on time.

cards.title: Permission and requests
cards.body: **Can I…? / Could I…? / May I…?** ask permission; **could** and **may** are more polite.
examples: Could you repeat the question, please?

items: I can to play the guitar.
I will be able to help you.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Asking the examiner to repeat politely is allowed and natural.
examples: Sorry, could you say that again, please?

practice.q: I ___ ride a bicycle when I was six.
After the training, she will [can] use the software.
Although the exam was difficult, I ___ (able) to finish it.
Which is correct?
Without a visa, you ___ enter the country.
Put the words in order.
practice.a: Could you repeat the question, please?

units.title: must, have to, should, need to

cards.title: Obligation and advice
cards.body:
- **must**: strong obligation, often the speaker's opinion or a rule
- **have to**: obligation from outside (rules, laws)
- **should / ought to**: advice or recommendation
- **need to**: necessity
examples: Governments should invest more in public transport.
Drivers have to wear seat belts.
We need to reduce plastic waste.

cards.title: Negatives are different
cards.body: **mustn't** = it is prohibited. **don't have to / don't need to** = it is not necessary.
examples: You mustn't use your phone in the exam.
You don't have to bring a pen; we provide one.

items: You mustn't come tomorrow — it's a holiday.
You don't have to come tomorrow — it's a holiday.
The government should invest in health.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Task 2 solution and opinion essays depend on **should**. Vary it with *ought to*, *it is essential that*, *it would be wise to*.
examples: Governments ought to make healthy food cheaper.
It is essential that children learn to manage money.

practice.q: In many countries, children ___ attend school until 16. It's the law.
You ___ smoke in the hospital.
It's free, so you ___ pay.
I think parents should [encouraging] children to read.
Governments ___ (ought) to provide free healthcare.
Which sentence is correct?
Put the words in order.
practice.a: Governments should invest more in renewable energy.

units.title: may, might, could, must, can't (possibility and deduction)
units.summary: How sure you are — and how to avoid sounding too certain.

cards.title: Degrees of certainty
cards.body:
- **must** = I'm almost sure it's true
- **may / might / could** = it's possible
- **can't** = I'm almost sure it's not true
examples: She must be tired — she worked all night.
This policy might reduce traffic.
That can't be right; the figures don't add up.

cards.title: Possibility in the past
cards.body: **must have / might have / can't have + past participle** for deductions about the past.
examples: He must have missed the bus.
They might have forgotten the meeting.

items: For deduction, the opposite of 'must' is 'can't'.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Strong band 7+ essays **hedge** claims: *may*, *could*, *might*, *is likely to*. 'Technology destroys families' is weaker than 'Technology may weaken family relationships'.
examples: Banning cars from city centres could improve air quality considerably.
Such measures might be unpopular at first.

practice.q: He's been running for an hour. He ___ be exhausted.
She's in Paris this week, so she ___ be at the meeting in Dhaka.
Which sentence is more academic?
o: Social media destroys teenagers' mental health.
Social media may harm some teenagers' mental health.
practice.a: Social media may harm some teenagers' mental health.
practice.x: Hedged, precise claims are stronger in Task 2.

practice.q: This policy could [reduces] unemployment.
The keys aren't here. I must ___ (leave) them in the car.
practice.x: Past deduction: must have + past participle.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: They might have forgot the date.
They might have forgotten the date.
practice.a: They might have forgotten the date.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Higher taxes on sugar could reduce obesity rates.

units.title: should have, could have, would have
units.summary: Regrets, criticism and unreal past possibilities.

cards.title: Looking back
cards.body:
- **should have + pp**: it was the right thing, but it didn't happen (regret/criticism)
- **could have + pp**: it was possible, but it didn't happen
- **would have + pp**: imagined past result (often with if)
examples: I should have started preparing earlier.
The government could have acted sooner.
I would have gone, but I was ill.

items: 'Of' is a spelling of the sound, not the grammar.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Part 2 cue cards often end with 'explain how you felt'. Past modals show reflection and grammatical range.
examples: Looking back, I should have asked for help much sooner.

practice.q: I failed the test. I ___ more.
We could have [took] a taxi, but we walked.
You should [of] told me earlier.
If I had known, I ___ (would / help) you.
Which sentence is correct?
o: The accident could have been avoided.
The accident could have be avoided.
practice.a: The accident could have been avoided.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: I should have booked the tickets earlier.

units.title: Verb + -ing or to-infinitive
units.summary: Which verbs are followed by -ing, which by to, and which by both.

cards.title: Verb + -ing
cards.body: **enjoy, avoid, consider, suggest, admit, deny, finish, mind, practise, risk, involve, keep, can't help**
examples: Many people avoid using public transport.
I suggest taking a short break.

cards.title: Verb + to-infinitive
cards.body: **want, decide, plan, hope, expect, agree, refuse, manage, afford, tend, fail, learn, aim, seem**
examples: Young people tend to spend more time online.
Many families cannot afford to buy a house.

cards.title: Both, with a change in meaning
cards.body: **stop, remember, forget, try**
examples: I stopped smoking. (I quit)
I stopped to smoke. (I paused in order to smoke)
Remember to lock the door. (future duty)
I remember locking the door. (memory of the past)

cards.title: After prepositions: always -ing
cards.body: After **in, of, about, by, without, before, instead of, interested in, good at, look forward to** use -ing.
examples: Instead of driving, more people should cycle.
I'm looking forward to hearing from you.

items: People should avoid to eat junk food.
People should avoid eating junk food.
They decided building a new road.
They decided to build a new road.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: These patterns appear in almost every Task 2 essay. Errors here are noticed quickly by examiners.
examples: Governments should consider introducing a sugar tax.
Many graduates struggle to find suitable jobs.

practice.q: I'm considering ___ abroad.
Many young people hope ___ a good job after university.
The government refused ___ (lower) taxes.
You can save money by ___ (cook) at home.
Children should avoid [to spend] too long on screens.
Most people cannot afford [buying] a house in the city.
On the way home, I stopped ___ some bread.
practice.x: Stop in order to do something.

practice.q: Which sentence is correct?
o: I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
practice.a: I look forward to meeting you.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Governments should encourage people to use public transport.

units.title: make, let, help, allow, encourage
units.summary: Verbs followed by an object and an infinitive — with or without 'to'.

cards.title: Without 'to'
cards.body: **make + object + base verb**, **let + object + base verb**, **help + object + (to) base verb**
examples: Strict rules make students work harder.
My parents let me choose my subject.
Technology helps people (to) communicate.

cards.title: With 'to'
cards.body: **allow, enable, encourage, force, persuade, require, want, ask, advise + object + to-infinitive**
examples: Online courses allow students to study at their own pace.
Higher prices may encourage people to buy less.

items: The internet allows people to communicate.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: These verbs describe causes and effects — the heart of many Task 2 arguments.
examples: Flexible working hours enable parents to spend more time with their children.

practice.q: Good teachers make lessons ___ interesting.
Scholarships enable poorer students ___ university.
Parents should not let children [to play] games all day.
The new law will force companies [reduce] emissions.
Which sentence is correct?
o: Smartphones allow us to stay connected.
Smartphones allow to us stay connected.
practice.a: Smartphones allow us to stay connected.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Free museums encourage people to learn about history.

units.title: The passive: forms
units.summary: Focus on the action or the result, not on who does it.

cards.title: When to use the passive
cards.body: Use the passive when **who does the action is unknown, unimportant or obvious**, or when you want to focus on the result.
examples: The bridge was built in 1998.
Millions of plastic bottles are thrown away every day.
The results will be announced next week.

items: English is speak in many countries.
English is spoken in many countries.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: The passive gives an objective, academic tone and shows grammatical range.
examples: More money should be spent on public health.
A new car park was built to the north of the station.

practice.q: Rice ___ (grow) in many parts of Asia.
The town hall ___ (destroy) by fire in 1950.
Several new schools ___ (build) since 2015.
Stricter laws should be [introduce] to protect wildlife.
The road is [repair] at the moment, so expect delays.
Which sentence is correct?
o: The winners will be announced tomorrow.
The winners will be announce tomorrow.
practice.a: The winners will be announced tomorrow.

practice.q: Rewrite in the passive: 'People recycle millions of tonnes of paper every year.'
practice.a: Millions of tonnes of paper are recycled every year.

units.title: The passive in academic writing
units.summary: Process diagrams, maps and impersonal reporting: 'It is believed that…'.

cards.title: Processes
cards.body: Describe each stage in the **present simple passive** with sequencing words.
examples: First, the leaves are picked by hand.
They are then dried and crushed.
Finally, the tea is packed and transported to shops.

cards.title: Maps
cards.body: Describe changes with the **past simple** or **present perfect passive**.
examples: The old factory was demolished.
A park has been created in place of the car park.

cards.title: Impersonal reporting
cards.body: **It is said / believed / thought / argued that…** and **X is believed to…** present views objectively.
examples: It is often argued that university education should be free.
Exercise is known to reduce stress.

items: The cocoa beans dry in the sun.
The cocoa beans are dried in the sun.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Process diagrams are almost impossible to describe well without the passive.
examples: Once the clay has been shaped, it is fired in a kiln at 1,000°C.

practice.q: Next, the mixture ___ (heat) to 200 degrees.
Between 1990 and 2010, the trees ___ (cut) down to make way for houses.
It ___ (widely / believe) that exercise improves memory.
After that, the bottles [fill] with water.
practice.x: The bottles don't fill themselves → passive.

practice.q: Smoking ___ to cause many diseases.
Which describes a map change correctly?
o: The library has been converted into a café.
The library has converted into a café.
The library converted into a café by them.
practice.a: The library has been converted into a café.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
practice.a: Finally, the finished products are delivered to supermarkets.

units.title: have / get something done
units.summary: Arranging for someone else to do something for you.

cards.title: Form and use
cards.body: **have / get + object + past participle** = someone does it for you.
examples: I had my hair cut yesterday.
We're getting our house painted.
You should get your eyes tested.

items: I cut my hair at the barber's.
I had my hair cut at the barber's.
Object comes before the past participle.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: A natural, less common structure that can lift Speaking grammar range.
examples: I usually get my clothes made by a local tailor.

practice.q: I need to ___ before the wedding.
She got her car [repair] last week.
We're having the kitchen ___ (paint).
Which sentence means someone else did it?
Put the words in order.
practice.a: I had my passport renewed last month.

units.title: Phrasal verbs and formal alternatives
units.summary: Use phrasal verbs in speaking; prefer formal verbs in essays.

cards.title: What they are
cards.body: A **verb + particle** with a new meaning: *give up* (stop), *look into* (investigate), *come up with* (think of).
examples: I gave up sugar last year.
We need to come up with a better plan.

cards.title: Use it in IELTS
cards.body: Natural phrasal verbs help **Speaking** Lexical Resource; formal single verbs suit **Task 1 and 2**.
examples: Speaking: I've taken up running recently.
Writing: Governments should conduct more research into renewable energy.

practice.q: Formal Task 2 version: 'We must cut down on plastic.'
'The meeting has been put off.' means…
Task 1: 'The number of visitors ___ from 2 to 5 million.'
Scientists carried ___ an experiment to test the theory.
Which is best in a formal essay?
o: The government should look into the problem.
The government should investigate the problem.
practice.a: The government should investigate the problem.

practice.q: Put the words in order.
